lines.text: religious feelings of gratitude which man experiences in
response to the beauty of nature are really awakened by the
presence of God and are directed towards Him. For nature
is His creation, and if with sensitive and true hearts we
honour the beauty of creation, we are in fact honouring
God the Creator. And yet if our devout thankfulness stops
at nature herself and does not go beyond her to the vision
of the Creator, then our religious response to nature is no
more than idolatry.
What is the real nature of the wrong which inheres in such
an attitude? It lies in the fact that by this attitude the
majesty of God is violated. God dwells in unapproachable
light (I Tim. 6: 16), and if He is present in nature He is also
concealed in nature. He does not allow Himself to be directly
seen by man—we can only believe in Him; and all the
splendours of nature and her teeming energies are not God
Himself, they do but point to God who, Himself unseen,
wraps Himself in the garb of nature. But the error of man is
this, that he wishes to look upon God and to hold un-
mediated communion with Him. And thus for him creation
becomes the Creator, the time of the world is equated with
eternity, and he forgets the significance of the word "While
the earth remains"
, and the limit it implies.
The fruits of this error are soon seen in the life of men, for
every wrong is avenged. We do not propose to dwell on the
way in which the error becomes most plainly visible. For in
fact man, who perhaps at first fostered genuinely religious
feelings of delight in nature, soon came to think that the
energies of nature whose inexhaustible power and abundance
he admires are divine, and when he remembers that his own
human being has its natural side-birth and growth, eating
and drinking, waking and sleeping—he easily succumbs to
the delusion that he too, man, is also a divine being. He feels
that a divine energy and a sacred will are expressed in his
blood, and in the impulses to which it gives rise. God lives
within him, he thinks, inasmuch as he belongs to the com-
munity of his people with its natural roots in race and soil,
